questions.title: Design a reusable research spike template for technology decisions
questions.quick: I use one template so every spike is comparable. It starts with the business question, a falsifiable hypothesis and success criteria, then fixes scope, candidates and a minimal prototype. Security review, functional and non-functional tests, cost and performance measurement, developer experience and operational complexity follow. It ends with findings and limits, a recommendation, an ADR and next steps. The time-box is fixed up front, and hypotheses are always kept separate from measured results.
questions.revision: One template: question, hypothesis, criteria, scope, candidates, prototype, security, tests, cost, experience, operations, findings, recommendation, ADR, next steps.
questions.detailed:
A spike is a time-boxed experiment that buys information, not a half-built product. A reusable template stops each evaluation being judged on different evidence.

{{diagram:spike-flow}}

## The template

| # | Section | What it must contain |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Business question | The decision being made and who owns it |
| 2 | Hypothesis | A falsifiable statement, for example "option A meets the latency target at lower run cost" |
| 3 | Success criteria | Numeric or observable thresholds agreed before building |
| 4 | Scope and exclusions | What is deliberately not tested |
| 5 | Candidates | Two or more options plus "do nothing" |
| 6 | Minimal prototype | The thinnest vertical slice that exercises the risky part |
| 7 | Security and compliance review | Identity, data residency, secrets, audit, licensing |
| 8 | Functional tests | Does it do the job on representative cases |
| 9 | Non-functional tests | Latency, throughput, reliability, limits, failure behaviour |
| 10 | Performance and cost measurement | Measured values with method and sample size |
| 11 | Developer experience | Time to first working feature, debugging, testing and tooling |
| 12 | Operational complexity | Deployment, monitoring, upgrades, on-call burden, skills needed |
| 13 | Findings and limits | What was learned, what was not tested, confidence level |
| 14 | Recommendation | One option, assumptions, and conditions that would change it |
| 15 | ADR and next steps | The decision record and the follow-up work |

## Rules that keep it honest

- **Hypotheses are not results.** Keep two columns: "Hypothesis" and "Measured". Use "<measured value>" until a number exists.
- **Fix the time-box first.** A typical spike is days, not weeks, with a named stop date.
- **Test the riskiest assumption first,** not the easiest demo.
- **State the limits.** A prototype on sample data says little about production scale.
- **Include a no-go outcome.** A spike that cannot fail is a demonstration.

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Choosing the winner before the spike and then collecting supporting evidence.
- Scoring only features and ignoring operations and cost.
- Letting the prototype quietly become the production system.
- Skipping the written record, so the question is reopened in six months.
followUps: How long should a spike last and who decides to stop it?
How do you stop a prototype becoming production code?
What do you record when a spike is inconclusive?

questions.title: Spike: Microsoft Agent Framework versus Semantic Kernel for an enterprise assistant
questions.quick: I would frame it as a time-boxed comparison on one bounded assistant use case, with the hypothesis written first: for example, that the newer framework gives simpler multi-agent orchestration while the older one has more mature connectors. I would build the same thin slice on both, then measure code size, test effort, observability, latency, token cost and migration risk. I record measured values separately, and verify current vendor docs for maturity and support status before recommending.
questions.revision: Same thin slice on both frameworks; hypotheses first, then measured effort, observability, cost and support status; verify vendor docs.
questions.detailed:
Both are Microsoft-ecosystem options for building agentic applications, and their relationship, maturity and roadmap have evolved. Treat any claim about which supersedes the other as something to verify in current vendor documentation, not something to assume.

## Business question and scope

Which framework should the AI centre of excellence standardise on as the default for building a bounded enterprise assistant with tool calling?

**Out of scope:** Model selection, prompt quality tuning, front-end design and production hardening of the assistant itself.

## Hypotheses versus measured results

Write the hypothesis before building anything, then record what was actually measured. Never present a hypothesis as a finding.

| Area | Hypothesis (before the spike) | Measured result |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestration simplicity | The newer framework needs less code for multi-step or multi-agent flows | <measured value> |
| Connector and plugin maturity | The established framework has more ready integrations | <measured value> |
| Observability | Both can emit OpenTelemetry-style traces, but setup effort differs | <measured value> |
| Test effort | Deterministic tool layers can be unit tested equally in both | <measured value> |
| Token cost and latency | Framework overhead is small compared with model calls | <measured value> |
| Support and roadmap risk | Needs checking against current vendor statements | <measured value> |

## Spike design

- Pick one use case with two tools and one human approval step.
- Implement the same behaviour in both, with the same model, prompts and tool code.
- Run a fixed set of 30 to 50 evaluation prompts and record success rate, latency and token usage.
- Time a developer new to each framework to a first working feature.
- Check tracing, logging, error handling and retry behaviour under injected tool failures.
- Review licensing, support commitments, release cadence and package stability.

## Decision rules

- Prefer the option meeting success criteria with lower operational effort, even if code is slightly longer.
- If results are within noise, choose by support status and team skills.
- If neither is stable enough, wrap tools behind your own interface and defer the choice.

## Draft ADR (fill in after measuring)

> **Decision:** Adopt <chosen framework> as the default for new assistants, behind a thin internal tool interface.
> **Status:** proposed, pending measured results and review.
> **Consequences:** Teams get one supported path; tool code stays portable; revisit when vendor support status changes.

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Comparing demos instead of the same measured slice.
- Ignoring the cost of migrating existing code.
- Treating preview features as production commitments.
- Quoting framework benchmarks from blogs as your own results.
followUps: How would you keep tool code portable between frameworks?
What if the vendor roadmap changes mid-spike?
How many evaluation prompts are enough?

questions.title: Spike: Power Automate versus Azure Functions for a complex approval workflow
questions.quick: I would build the same approval workflow with branching, retries and one external API call in both, after writing hypotheses: Power Automate wins on delivery speed and maker ownership, Functions on testability, version control and throughput control. Then I measure build time, test coverage, run cost per thousand executions, failure handling, and the effort to deploy through environments. Results go in a table separate from the hypotheses, and licensing needs checking in current vendor docs.
questions.revision: Build one workflow both ways; compare build time, testability, run cost, failure handling and ALM effort, keeping hypotheses and measurements separate.
questions.detailed:
This spike compares a low-code flow engine with code-first serverless for a workflow that has outgrown simple automation.

## Business question and scope

For an approval workflow with parallel branches, retries, external calls and audit needs, which platform gives the better balance of speed, control and run cost?

**Out of scope:** Front-end approval UI, identity provider changes and enterprise-wide platform governance.

## Hypotheses versus measured results

Write the hypothesis before building anything, then record what was actually measured. Never present a hypothesis as a finding.

| Area | Hypothesis (before the spike) | Measured result |
|---|---|---|
| Delivery speed | Power Automate is faster to first working version | <measured value> |
| Testability | Functions allow unit and integration tests in a pipeline | <measured value> |
| Source control and review | Functions diff cleanly; flows depend on solution export tooling | <measured value> |
| Throughput and limits | Functions offer more control; flows have platform limits to verify | <measured value> |
| Run cost | Depends on licensing model and volume, which must be calculated | <measured value> |
| Ownership | Makers can maintain flows; Functions need developers | <measured value> |

## Spike design

- Define one workflow with at least four steps, a parallel branch and a compensating action.
- Implement it in both, using the same external API stub.
- Inject failures: timeout, duplicate trigger and malformed payload.
- Measure build hours, lines or actions, and time to diagnose an injected failure.
- Run a load of <target volume> executions and capture duration and throttling.
- Deploy each through dev, test and production using the intended ALM route.

## Decision rules

- If volume and complexity are low and makers own it, prefer the flow.
- If testing, throughput or code review dominate, prefer Functions.
- A hybrid with flows calling Functions is a valid third outcome.

## Draft ADR (fill in after measuring)

> **Decision:** Use <option> for workflows meeting <criteria>; use <other option> where <criteria>.
> **Status:** proposed, pending measured results and review.
> **Consequences:** Two supported patterns need clear selection guidance and an owner for each.

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Comparing licence price only and ignoring maintenance effort.
- Measuring happy paths and skipping failure behaviour.
- Forgetting who will be on call for the result.
followUps: How would a hybrid pattern work?
How would you measure maintainability?
Who owns the run when makers built it?

questions.title: Spike: Databricks Genie versus a custom analytics assistant
questions.quick: I would pick five to ten real business questions with known correct answers and run them through both. The hypothesis, written first, is that the managed option reaches acceptable accuracy faster on well-modelled data, while a custom assistant gives more control over prompts, guardrails and UX. I measure answer accuracy, latency, cost, permission enforcement and maintenance effort as separate results, and verify current Genie capabilities and licensing in vendor docs.
questions.revision: Run real questions with known answers through both; compare accuracy, permissions, latency, cost and maintenance, keeping hypotheses apart from results.
questions.detailed:
Natural-language analytics is a build-or-adopt question. A spike on real questions beats opinion.

## Business question and scope

Can a managed conversational analytics feature answer our governed business questions accurately enough, or do we need a custom assistant?

**Out of scope:** Data modelling programme, dashboard redesign and any write-back to source systems.

## Hypotheses versus measured results

Write the hypothesis before building anything, then record what was actually measured. Never present a hypothesis as a finding.

| Area | Hypothesis (before the spike) | Measured result |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy on curated questions | Managed option is good when tables are well described | <measured value> |
| Accuracy on ambiguous questions | Custom prompts and semantic layer may do better | <measured value> |
| Permission enforcement | Managed option inherits catalogue permissions | <measured value> |
| Latency | Similar, dominated by query execution | <measured value> |
| Cost | Depends on compute and licensing, to be measured | <measured value> |
| Maintenance | Managed option has fewer moving parts | <measured value> |

## Spike design

- Collect 20 real questions from business users with agreed correct answers.
- Prepare table and column descriptions once and reuse them for both.
- Score each answer as correct, partly correct or wrong, and record the SQL.
- Test row and column permissions with two different user roles.
- Measure median and slowest response time and compute cost per question.
- Record the effort needed to add a new metric or fix a wrong answer.

## Decision rules

- Adopt the managed option if accuracy meets the target on governed data.
- Build custom only where a measured gap matters to the business.
- Always keep a human-reviewable SQL view.

## Draft ADR (fill in after measuring)

> **Decision:** Use <managed or custom> for governed analytics questions, with a review process for wrong answers.
> **Status:** proposed, pending measured results and review.
> **Consequences:** Data teams own descriptions and curated questions either way.

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Testing with questions the team already knows will work.
- Skipping permission tests.
- Counting build effort but not the ongoing tuning effort.
followUps: How do you score an answer that is partly correct?
How would you handle ambiguous metrics?
What is the fallback when accuracy drops?

questions.title: Spike: PAC CLI-based deployment versus native Power Platform Pipelines
questions.quick: I would deploy the same solution through both routes across development, test and production and compare. The hypothesis is that native pipelines give the lowest setup effort and maker-friendly approvals, while CLI-based automation gives richer testing, branching and integration with existing release tooling. I measure setup time, deployment duration, failure recovery, auditability and skill demands separately, and verify current vendor docs because capabilities change.
questions.revision: Deploy one solution through both routes; compare setup effort, duration, rollback, audit and skills, recording hypotheses apart from measurements.
questions.detailed:
Both routes move solutions between environments. They differ in who operates them and how much control they give.

## Business question and scope

Which deployment route should be the default for solutions across environments?

**Out of scope:** Environment strategy, licensing decisions and a full redesign of release governance.

## Hypotheses versus measured results

Write the hypothesis before building anything, then record what was actually measured. Never present a hypothesis as a finding.

| Area | Hypothesis (before the spike) | Measured result |
|---|---|---|
| Setup effort | Native pipelines need less setup | <measured value> |
| Pipeline flexibility | CLI automation supports custom steps and tests | <measured value> |
| Approvals and audit | Both can provide them, differently | <measured value> |
| Rollback | Needs testing, since solution rollback is limited | <measured value> |
| Skills | Native suits makers; CLI needs engineering skills | <measured value> |
| Source control | CLI route fits git-based review more naturally | <measured value> |

## Spike design

- Choose one solution with a flow, a table change and an environment variable.
- Deploy it dev to test to production by both routes.
- Break the deployment on purpose with a missing dependency and record recovery.
- Time setup, first deployment and a repeat deployment.
- Check what evidence each route keeps for audit.
- Document each route's prerequisites and permissions.

## Decision rules

- Default to native pipelines if they meet audit and testing needs.
- Use external orchestration where automated tests, branching or cross-system releases are required.
- A hybrid with a standard wrapper is acceptable if owned.

## Draft ADR (fill in after measuring)

> **Decision:** Use <route> as the default release path for solutions, with documented exceptions.
> **Status:** proposed, pending measured results and review.
> **Consequences:** One supported path simplifies support; exceptions need approval.

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Comparing a perfect demo only.
- Ignoring service principal and permission setup effort.
- Assuming rollback is trivial.
followUps: How do you handle rollback of a solution deployment?
Who should approve production deployments?
When does a hybrid make sense?

questions.title: Spike: Power Apps code app versus a model-driven app for an internal tool
questions.quick: I would build one representative internal tool, a case list with a form, a custom visual and one workflow action, in both. The hypothesis is that the model-driven app gets there faster with built-in security, views and forms, while a code app gives complete UI control and standard web tooling. I measure build time, UI fit, security behaviour, test effort and maintenance separately, and verify current vendor docs because code app capabilities and status may change.
questions.revision: Build one internal tool both ways; compare build time, UI fit, security, testability and upkeep, separating hypotheses from measurements.
questions.detailed:
The choice is between a configuration-driven shell on Dataverse and a custom front end that still runs on the platform.

## Business question and scope

For this internal tool, does the required UI justify custom code, or does a model-driven app meet the need?

**Out of scope:** Data model redesign, mobile offline needs and external-user portals.

## Hypotheses versus measured results

Write the hypothesis before building anything, then record what was actually measured. Never present a hypothesis as a finding.

| Area | Hypothesis (before the spike) | Measured result |
|---|---|---|
| Build time | Model-driven is quicker for table-centric screens | <measured value> |
| UI flexibility | Code app handles bespoke interaction | <measured value> |
| Security | Model-driven inherits table security directly | <measured value> |
| Testing | Code app supports standard front-end tests | <measured value> |
| Accessibility | Built-in components have a head start | <measured value> |
| Upkeep | Code needs developers and dependency updates | <measured value> |

## Spike design

- List the five screens or behaviours the users actually need.
- Build the highest-risk screen first in each approach.
- Check role-based access with two different users.
- Write automated tests where the approach allows.
- Record developer hours and defects found by testers.
- Review supportability: who fixes it when the author leaves.

## Decision rules

- Choose model-driven when most needs are forms, views and processes.
- Choose a code app only when a named requirement cannot be met otherwise.
- Re-evaluate when the platform adds capabilities.

## Draft ADR (fill in after measuring)

> **Decision:** Use <approach> for <tool class>, with code apps requiring a stated UI justification.
> **Status:** proposed, pending measured results and review.
> **Consequences:** Developers own code apps; makers can support model-driven ones.

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Choosing code for visual preference alone.
- Forgetting accessibility and security work in the code path.
- Comparing only the first screen.
followUps: How would you test the code app's security?
What UI need would justify custom code?
How do you handle a code app when its author leaves?

questions.title: Spike: AI-assisted versus conventional development for a bounded feature
questions.quick: I would pick one bounded feature and have comparable engineers deliver it both ways, or the same engineer on two similar features. The hypothesis is that AI assistance speeds delivery but needs stronger review and testing. I measure elapsed time, review effort, defects found, test coverage and rework as results, never citing industry numbers as our own, and record security and licensing review. The sample is tiny, so I state the limits.
questions.revision: Deliver one bounded feature both ways; compare time, review effort, defects and rework, state sample limits, and never present hypotheses as results.
questions.detailed:
Productivity claims for AI coding assistants vary widely, so an internal spike should measure our context.

## Business question and scope

Does AI-assisted development improve delivery of a bounded feature without lowering quality or raising risk?

**Out of scope:** Whole-team productivity claims, tool procurement and long-term skills development.

## Hypotheses versus measured results

Write the hypothesis before building anything, then record what was actually measured. Never present a hypothesis as a finding.

| Area | Hypothesis (before the spike) | Measured result |
|---|---|---|
| Elapsed time | AI assistance reduces time to first working version | <measured value> |
| Review effort | Reviewers spend longer per change | <measured value> |
| Defects | Defect rate is similar if tests are required | <measured value> |
| Test coverage | Higher if the tool drafts tests | <measured value> |
| Rework | May rise if prompts were vague | <measured value> |
| Security findings | Needs scanning either way | <measured value> |

## Spike design

- Choose two similar bounded features with clear acceptance tests.
- Apply the same definition of done, scans and review rules to both.
- Record time on coding, review, fixes and tests.
- Log defects found in review, testing and the first two weeks.
- Check generated code for licence, secrets and dependency risk.
- Ask developers about experience and where they distrusted output.

## Decision rules

- Adopt where quality metrics hold and review effort is acceptable.
- Require human review of every generated change.
- Treat a single spike as a signal, not proof.

## Draft ADR (fill in after measuring)

> **Decision:** Allow AI-assisted development for <class of work> with mandatory tests, review and scanning.
> **Status:** proposed, pending measured results and review.
> **Consequences:** Guidelines on data handling and review need maintaining.

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Using lines of code as the measure.
- Letting the keenest engineer do the AI path and the least keen do the other.
- Quoting vendor studies as local evidence.
followUps: How would you control for engineer skill?
What would make you stop using it for a class of work?
How do you handle licence risk in generated code?

questions.title: How do you balance research spikes with committed Kanban delivery?
questions.quick: I treat spikes as explicit work items with a time-box, an owner and a question, not hidden side work. I give them a dedicated lane or a capped share of capacity, apply work-in-progress limits, and keep an expedite path for committed delivery. Each spike ends with a decision, not a prototype. I review the ratio of spikes to delivery regularly, and stop any spike that overruns without new information.
questions.revision: Make spikes visible, time-boxed work items with WIP limits and a capacity cap, ending in a decision, with an expedite lane protecting commitments.
questions.detailed:
The risk is that research either starves delivery or becomes an invisible second job.

{{diagram:kanban-lane}}

## Practical approach

1. **Make spikes first-class cards.** Each has a question, owner, time-box and expected decision.
2. **Cap capacity.** For example, reserve a share of throughput, such as <agreed percentage>, based on your own flow data.
3. **Apply WIP limits.** One or two spikes at a time, so they finish.
4. **Protect commitments.** An expedite or service-class rule lets committed items pre-empt a spike.
5. **Define done.** A spike ends with a recommendation and ADR, or an explicit "inconclusive, here is what we learned".
6. **Feed delivery.** A positive result creates normal backlog items sized from what was learned.

## Policies to agree with stakeholders

| Policy | Example |
|---|---|
| Entry | A named decision depends on it and a sponsor agrees |
| Time-box | Fixed on the card; extension needs a new decision |
| Service class | Spikes are standard, never expedite |
| Exit | Decision recorded, prototype archived or deleted |
| Review | Monthly check of spike outcomes and cycle time |

## Measuring balance

Use flow metrics: cycle time of committed items before and after introducing spikes, blocked time, and the proportion of spikes that led to a decision. If committed cycle time rises, reduce the cap.

## Handling pressure

If a delivery deadline collides with a spike, pause the spike and record the open question rather than cutting the evidence short and presenting a guess as a finding.

## Practical tip

Write the decision, the evidence behind it and the conditions for revisiting it in one short page, share it with the people affected before the meeting, and keep a dated log so the reasoning can be audited later.

## Common mistakes

- Running spikes without a time-box so they expand to fill capacity.
- Starting a spike with no decision waiting for it.
- Letting prototype code flow into production without hardening.
- Hiding spike work, then explaining delays afterwards.
followUps: What share of capacity would you reserve and why?
What do you do when a spike overruns?
How do you show stakeholders the cost of spikes?

diagrams.title: Spikes in a Kanban system
diagrams.alt: Incoming requests are triaged. Committed delivery items go through the normal lane. Spike items enter a capped spike lane with a time-box, end in a decision, and may create new delivery items.

questions.title: How do you present a spike outcome to executives?
questions.quick: I lead with the decision requested and the recommendation in one sentence, then the business impact: cost, risk, time and who is affected. I show two or three options in a short comparison, the evidence with clear separation between measured results and assumptions, the limits of the spike, and what would change my recommendation. I finish with the ask, next steps and an owner. Detail goes in an appendix and the ADR.
questions.revision: Lead with the decision and recommendation, show options and evidence separately from assumptions, state limits and what would change it, end with the ask.
questions.detailed:
Executives need a decision they can take with known risk, not a tour of the experiment.

{{diagram:exec-story}}

## Structure for a one-page summary

1. **Decision and recommendation.** "We recommend <option> for <scope>, subject to <condition>."
2. **Why it matters.** Cost, delivery time, risk, compliance and customer impact in plain terms.
3. **Options.** Two or three, including doing nothing.
4. **Evidence.** What was measured, with the method, and separately what is assumed.
5. **Limits.** What the spike did not test and the confidence level.
6. **What would change the recommendation.** Named triggers.
7. **The ask.** Budget, approval or a further time-boxed step, with an owner and date.

## Example comparison

| Option | Cost to deliver | Run cost | Risk | Fit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | <measured value> | <measured value> | Low | Meets criteria |
| B | <measured value> | <measured value> | Medium | Partly meets |
| Do nothing | None | Rising | High | Fails criteria |

## Communication practices

- Use their vocabulary, not framework names.
- Label estimates as estimates and measurements as measurements.
- Pre-wire the sponsor so there are no surprises.
- Be explicit when the spike was inconclusive and say what would resolve it.
- Offer the ADR as the record, not a slide deck of detail.

## Practical tip

Write the decision, the evidence behind it and the conditions for revisiting it in one short page, share it with the people affected before the meeting, and keep a dated log so the reasoning can be audited later.

## Common mistakes

- Beginning with architecture diagrams instead of the decision.
- Presenting a prototype demo as proof of production readiness.
- Hiding limits or negative results.
- Giving a single option with no alternatives.
- Using unverified numbers from vendor material as if they were results.
followUps: How do you handle an executive who wants a different answer?
How do you present an inconclusive spike?
What goes in the appendix?

diagrams.title: Executive spike summary
diagrams.alt: A one-page executive summary moves from the decision requested and recommendation to options and evidence, then limits and risks, and ends with the ask and next steps, with the ADR as an appendix.

questions.title: Trade-off: Power Automate or Azure Functions for a business workflow?
questions.quick: There is no universal answer, so I ask about volume, complexity, who maintains it and how it must be tested. For low-to-medium volume, maker-owned processes with standard connectors I would use Power Automate; for high throughput, complex logic, strict testing or tight cost control I would use Azure Functions; a hybrid is often best. I would document it in an ADR with the evidence that would change it, such as run-cost data or flow limits.
questions.revision: Flows for maker-owned, connector-heavy, moderate-volume work; Functions for complex, high-volume, test-critical work; hybrid is common. Record in an ADR.
questions.detailed:
A common platform-choice question where context decides.

{{diagram:pa-vs-fn}}

## Business context

An operations team wants a multi-step approval and data synchronisation process. Today it is spreadsheets and email.

## Clarifying questions

- How many executions per day and what peak?
- Who will maintain it after delivery?
- What audit and testing evidence is required?
- Which systems have ready connectors?
- What is the tolerance for failure and duplicates?

## Constraints

- Existing licensing and tenant policies.
- Team skills in low-code versus code.
- Data residency and secrets handling.
- Release process already in place.

## Options

| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Power Automate | Fast delivery, connectors, maker ownership | Platform limits, harder code review and testing, licence-driven cost |
| Azure Functions | Full control, testing, source control, scalable | Needs developers, more operations work |
| Hybrid | Flow orchestrates, Function handles complex step | Two things to run and support |

## Operational and organisational trade-offs

- Ownership: makers can fix flows but may bypass review; developers own Functions but become a bottleneck.
- Operations: Functions need monitoring and deployment pipelines you must build; flows use platform tooling.
- Cost: compare licensing against compute at your volume using real figures.
- Governance: both need naming, environment and connection standards.

## Recommendation under stated assumptions

**Assumptions:** Moderate volume, standard connectors, a team of makers with developer support, and moderate audit needs.

**Recommendation:** Start with Power Automate for the standard path and move a step to Azure Functions only when logic or throughput exceeds what the flow handles cleanly.

## Evidence that would change the recommendation

- Measured throttling or limit breaches.
- Run-cost comparison at real volume.
- A need for automated tests the flow cannot support.
- Maintenance burden showing in incident data.

## ADR

```markdown
# ADR: Workflow engine for approval process
Status: Proposed
Context: Operations process, moderate volume, maker-owned.
Decision: Use Power Automate; extract complex steps to Azure Functions behind an HTTP interface.
Consequences: Two skill sets; clear boundary needed.
Revisit when: Volume or limits exceed agreed thresholds.
```

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Treating low-code as always cheaper or always worse.
- Ignoring who is on call.
- Forgetting retries and idempotency in either choice.
followUps: What would trigger moving a step out of the flow?
How would you test a flow?
How do you prevent duplicate processing?

diagrams.title: Choosing a workflow engine
diagrams.alt: A request to automate a process is assessed for volume and complexity, ownership and testing needs. It routes to a Power Automate flow, an Azure Function, or a hybrid where a flow calls a function for the complex step.

questions.title: Trade-off: Dataverse or Azure SQL/PostgreSQL for application data?
questions.quick: I would ask who builds on the data, what scale and query patterns are needed, and how security and integration must work. Dataverse suits Power Platform apps needing built-in security, auditing and low-code access; Azure SQL or PostgreSQL suit large volumes, complex queries, multi-consumer systems and cost control. I would pick by workload, avoid dual sources of truth, and write an ADR that names the evidence that would change it, such as capacity and licensing costs.
questions.revision: Dataverse for Power Platform-centred apps with built-in security; SQL or PostgreSQL for heavy queries, many consumers and cost control. Avoid two sources of truth.
questions.detailed:
Where the system of record lives shapes everything else, so the answer depends on the workload.

## Business context

A new internal application will be used mainly by business users through Power Platform, but several services also need its data.

## Clarifying questions

- Expected rows, growth and query complexity?
- Who consumes the data beyond the app?
- What security model is needed, row level or table level?
- Is reporting mixed with transactional use?
- What licensing is already in place?

## Constraints

- Storage and API limits to verify in vendor docs.
- Existing data platform standards.
- Audit and retention rules.
- Team skills.

## Options

| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Dataverse | Built-in security, audit, forms, flows, low-code | Capacity cost, API limits, less suited to heavy analytical queries |
| Azure SQL or PostgreSQL | Rich querying, scale, tooling, portability | You build security, APIs and app integration |
| Dataverse for app state plus a relational store for heavy data | Fits each workload | Synchronisation and ownership complexity |

## Operational and organisational trade-offs

- Delivery speed favours Dataverse for Power Platform apps.
- Integration breadth and query power favour a relational database.
- Organisationally, a platform team must own whichever is chosen.
- Moving later is costly, so choose the system of record deliberately.

## Recommendation under stated assumptions

**Assumptions:** Power Platform is the primary front end, moderate data volume and few outside consumers.

**Recommendation:** Use Dataverse as the system of record; expose a read-optimised copy to analytics rather than a second writable store.

## Evidence that would change the recommendation

- Capacity projections that make licensing expensive.
- Query patterns that need joins Dataverse handles poorly.
- Many non-platform consumers needing direct access.
- API limit breaches in testing.

## ADR

```markdown
# ADR: System of record for the application
Status: Proposed
Context: Power Platform app with moderate volume.
Decision: Dataverse as the single writable store; analytics via replicated copy.
Consequences: Capacity and API limits monitored.
Revisit when: Volume or consumers exceed assumptions.
```

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Writing the same data in two stores.
- Choosing by preference rather than workload.
- Ignoring capacity cost until after launch.
followUps: How would you migrate if you outgrew Dataverse?
How do you serve analytics?
What security gaps appear with a relational store?

questions.title: Trade-off: model-driven app or code app for a new business application?
questions.quick: I start by asking what screens users really need, how bespoke the interaction is, who will maintain it and what accessibility and security demands exist. Table-centric work with views, forms and approvals favours a model-driven app; a distinctive interaction model favours a code app or a standard web app. I recommend the least custom option that meets named requirements, record an ADR, and revisit if requirements change.
questions.revision: Model-driven for table-centred forms and views; code app when a named UI need demands it; pick the least custom option meeting the requirements.
questions.detailed:
A build-versus-configure decision, repeated for every new application.

## Business context

A case management tool for 300 staff with search, forms, dashboards and one interactive planning board.

## Clarifying questions

- How many screens are bespoke?
- Who maintains it after launch?
- Accessibility and device requirements?
- Is offline needed?
- Does it need to follow a corporate design?

## Constraints

- Platform capabilities and status to verify in current docs.
- Developer availability.
- Security reviews.
- Time to first release.

## Options

| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Model-driven app | Fast, built-in security and accessibility | Limited layout freedom |
| Code app | Full UI control, normal web tooling | Developer ownership, more testing and upkeep |
| Model-driven with an embedded custom component | Standard shell, custom only where needed | Component lifecycle to manage |

## Operational and organisational trade-offs

- Maker versus developer ownership affects support cost.
- Custom code brings dependency updates and security patching.
- Standard components improve consistency across apps.
- Hiring and training differ between the two.

## Recommendation under stated assumptions

**Assumptions:** Most screens are standard, with one custom board.

**Recommendation:** Model-driven shell with a single custom component for the board; avoid a full code app until more than a few screens need bespoke behaviour.

## Evidence that would change the recommendation

- Most screens turn out to be bespoke.
- User testing rejects the standard layout.
- Component maintenance costs exceed estimates.
- Platform capability changes.

## ADR

```markdown
# ADR: Front-end approach for case management
Status: Proposed
Context: Mostly table-centred screens with one custom view.
Decision: Model-driven app plus one custom component.
Consequences: Developers own the component; makers own the rest.
Revisit when: Custom screens exceed an agreed number.
```

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Building custom because it looks better in a demo.
- Underestimating accessibility work.
- Ignoring who patches dependencies.
followUps: How do you decide when a component is too big?
How would you test accessibility?
What changes if external users are added?

questions.title: Trade-off: agent framework or deterministic workflow for an automation task?
questions.quick: I ask whether the steps are known in advance, what an error costs, and whether the input is genuinely open-ended. If the path is known and auditable, a deterministic workflow is cheaper, faster and easier to test; if the task needs flexible tool choice over unstructured input, an agent can help, ideally inside guardrails. Often the best design is a workflow with one model-driven step. I would record this in an ADR.
questions.revision: Known, auditable steps favour deterministic workflows; open-ended input needing tool choice favours agents; often a workflow with one model step wins.
questions.detailed:
Agents are not a default; they are a tool for uncertainty.

{{diagram:agent-or-flow}}

## Business context

A support team wants to triage incoming requests, look up accounts and draft replies.

## Clarifying questions

- Are the steps fixed?
- What happens when it is wrong?
- Is human review in the loop?
- What volume and latency matter?
- What must be auditable?

## Constraints

- Cost per run.
- Evaluation capability.
- Security of tool access.
- Explainability requirements.

## Options

| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Deterministic workflow | Predictable, cheap, testable, auditable | Poor with unstructured variation |
| Autonomous agent | Flexible tool use, handles variation | Variable cost and behaviour, harder to test |
| Workflow with a model step for classification or drafting | Bounded model use, clear control | Needs good evaluation of the model step |

## Operational and organisational trade-offs

- Operations: agents need tracing and evaluation sets.
- Organisation: owners must accept probabilistic behaviour.
- Cost: loops and retries can inflate token use.
- Safety: tools need least privilege.

## Recommendation under stated assumptions

**Assumptions:** Triage categories are known, replies need review, and errors are moderately costly.

**Recommendation:** Use a deterministic workflow with a model step for classification and draft generation, and human approval before sending.

## Evidence that would change the recommendation

- Evaluation showing the model step alone is insufficient.
- A large share of requests needing unplanned tool sequences.
- Evidence that guardrails hold under test.

## ADR

```markdown
# ADR: Automation style for support triage
Status: Proposed
Context: Known steps, unstructured text input.
Decision: Workflow with bounded model steps and approval.
Consequences: Less autonomy, more predictability.
Revisit when: Evaluation shows agents outperform within risk limits.
```

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Using an agent because it is fashionable.
- No evaluation set.
- Giving tools broad permissions.
followUps: How would you evaluate the model step?
What guardrails would an agent need?
How do you cap cost?

diagrams.title: Agent or workflow decision
diagrams.alt: A task is assessed for whether steps are known. Known steps go to a deterministic workflow. Unknown steps with low risk go to an agent with guardrails. Mixed tasks use a workflow containing one model step.

questions.title: Trade-off: single agent or multi-agent design?
questions.quick: I would start with a single agent and clear tools, because every extra agent adds latency, cost, failure modes and evaluation effort. I move to multiple agents only when there is a measured reason: distinct permissions, separable skills with different prompts or models, or parallel independent work. I ask about complexity of tasks and security boundaries, test both on a representative set, and record an ADR with the evidence that would justify splitting.
questions.revision: Start with one agent; split only for distinct permissions, separable skills or parallel work, proven by evaluation, because each agent adds cost and failure modes.
questions.detailed:
Multi-agent systems look elegant on diagrams, but coordination is a real cost.

## Business context

A research assistant that gathers internal documents, queries data and drafts summaries.

## Clarifying questions

- Do sub-tasks need different permissions?
- Are sub-tasks independent and parallelisable?
- What is the latency budget?
- How will we evaluate the result?
- Who debugs multi-agent traces?

## Constraints

- Token budget.
- Observability tooling.
- Security boundaries between data sources.
- Team experience.

## Options

| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Single agent with several tools | Simple, cheap, easy to trace | Long context, tool confusion if too many tools |
| Orchestrator with specialist agents | Separation of skills and permissions | Latency, cost, coordination errors |
| Workflow with fixed stages, each a bounded model call | Predictable, testable | Less adaptive |

## Operational and organisational trade-offs

- Operations: traces must follow handoffs.
- Organisation: ownership of each agent must be clear.
- Evaluation effort multiplies with agent count.
- Security can improve by isolating tool access.

## Recommendation under stated assumptions

**Assumptions:** Tasks are moderately complex, one permission boundary and a modest latency budget.

**Recommendation:** Single agent with a small tool set, and a workflow stage structure if tools grow; split only where permissions differ.

## Evidence that would change the recommendation

- Tool selection errors rising with tool count.
- A separate data source needing isolated credentials.
- Measured gain from parallelism.
- Evaluation showing specialist prompts outperform.

## ADR

```markdown
# ADR: Agent topology for the research assistant
Status: Proposed
Context: One permission boundary, moderate complexity.
Decision: Single agent; split on permission boundaries.
Consequences: Simpler operations; may need refactoring.
Revisit when: Tool count or permission needs change.
```

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Splitting agents by job title instead of need.
- No handoff tracing.
- Measuring demos not evaluation sets.
followUps: How would you trace a multi-agent run?
What if latency doubles with the split?
How do you cap runaway loops?

questions.title: Trade-off: managed Power Platform components or custom code?
questions.quick: I ask what the requirement really is, how stable it will be, and who will support it. Managed components such as built-in connectors, standard controls and platform features are cheaper to run and upgrade automatically, but may constrain behaviour; custom code gives control at the cost of ownership. I choose the managed option by default, custom code when a measured gap or requirement justifies it, and write an ADR naming the gap.
questions.revision: Default to managed components for lower upkeep; use custom code only for a named, measured gap, with an owner and an ADR.
questions.detailed:
Every line of custom code is a long-term obligation.

## Business context

A team needs a validation step and a data display that platform features nearly, but not exactly, cover.

## Clarifying questions

- What exactly is the gap?
- How stable is the requirement?
- Who maintains custom code?
- Could process change remove the need?
- What are the security implications?

## Constraints

- Upgrade cadence of the platform.
- Skills available.
- Testing capability.
- Support model.

## Options

| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Managed components only | Low upkeep, upgrades included | Requirement may be compromised |
| Custom code for the gap | Exact behaviour | Ownership, testing, upgrade risk |
| Change the process to fit the platform | Cheapest in the long run | Needs business agreement |

## Operational and organisational trade-offs

- Custom code needs patching, testing and documentation.
- Platform upgrades can break custom extensions.
- Business may value the exact behaviour more than lower cost.
- Support skills may be scarce.

## Recommendation under stated assumptions

**Assumptions:** Requirement is moderately stable and developers are available but limited.

**Recommendation:** Use managed components, negotiate the process where possible, and build the smallest custom piece only for gaps that remain, with tests and an owner.

## Evidence that would change the recommendation

- Business case for the exact behaviour.
- Repeated workarounds that cost more than code.
- Platform changes that close the gap.

## ADR

```markdown
# ADR: Custom extension for validation
Status: Proposed
Context: Platform nearly meets the need.
Decision: Build a minimal, tested extension for the remaining gap.
Consequences: Named owner and upgrade checks.
Revisit when: Platform adds equivalent capability.
```

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Custom code as a first resort.
- No tests for extensions.
- No owner after the author leaves.
followUps: How do you decide a gap is real?
How do you test extensions across platform updates?
Who owns custom code?

questions.title: Trade-off: synchronous API or asynchronous messaging between systems?
questions.quick: I ask whether the caller needs an immediate answer, how reliable the downstream system is, what volume spikes look like and how failure should be handled. Synchronous APIs are simpler and give immediate feedback but couple availability; asynchronous messaging absorbs spikes and failures but adds eventual consistency and operational pieces. I would use sync for queries and short commands, async for long or bursty work, and record this in an ADR.
questions.revision: Sync for immediate answers and simplicity; async for spikes, slow or unreliable downstreams and decoupling, accepting eventual consistency. Mix by use case.
questions.detailed:
Integration style decides failure behaviour as much as the data model does.

{{diagram:sync-async}}

## Business context

An order process calls a slow partner system and occasionally faces peak bursts.

## Clarifying questions

- Does the user need the result now?
- What is the partner's availability and rate limit?
- Can processing be duplicated safely?
- What ordering is required?
- How will failures be surfaced?

## Constraints

- Partner limits.
- Existing messaging platform.
- Team skills.
- Audit requirements.

## Options

| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Synchronous API | Simple, immediate feedback | Tight coupling, cascading failure, timeouts |
| Asynchronous messaging | Buffers bursts, retries, decoupled | Eventual consistency, idempotency, monitoring of queues |
| Sync acknowledgement with async processing | User gets a receipt, work completes later | Needs status tracking |

## Operational and organisational trade-offs

- Operations: queues need depth and dead-letter monitoring.
- Organisation: teams must agree message contracts.
- Users must accept pending states.
- Debugging distributed flows needs correlation IDs.

## Recommendation under stated assumptions

**Assumptions:** The partner is slow and bursty, and the user can accept a pending status.

**Recommendation:** Accept the request synchronously, process asynchronously with idempotent consumers, retries and a dead-letter queue, and show status.

## Evidence that would change the recommendation

- Partner becoming fast and reliable.
- Users needing immediate confirmation of the final result.
- Operational burden of messaging exceeding value.

## ADR

```markdown
# ADR: Integration style for partner calls
Status: Proposed
Context: Slow, bursty partner.
Decision: Async processing with synchronous acknowledgement.
Consequences: Status tracking and idempotency required.
Revisit when: Partner behaviour changes.
```

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Retrying non-idempotent operations.
- No dead-letter handling.
- Hiding pending states from users.
followUps: How do you make consumers idempotent?
How do you monitor a queue?
What ordering guarantees do you need?

diagrams.title: Sync versus async path
diagrams.alt: A caller sends a request. If an immediate answer is needed the call goes directly to the API. Otherwise the message goes to a queue, a consumer processes it with retries and a dead-letter path, and the caller is notified of completion.

questions.title: Trade-off: shared or isolated environments for teams and applications?
questions.quick: I ask about data sensitivity, team autonomy, release cadence, and the admin capacity to manage many environments. Shared environments are cheaper and simpler to administer but couple releases, permissions and blast radius; isolated environments give clean boundaries and independent lifecycles at higher management cost. I would isolate by sensitivity and lifecycle, share where risk is low, and document a clear environment strategy in an ADR.
questions.revision: Isolate by data sensitivity, lifecycle and blast radius; share where risk is low and admin capacity is limited; document the strategy.
questions.detailed:
Environment strategy is a governance decision, not just a technical one.

## Business context

Several teams are building apps and automations, some handling confidential data.

## Clarifying questions

- Which apps handle sensitive data?
- How often does each team release?
- Who administers environments?
- What are licensing and capacity implications?
- What DLP boundaries exist?

## Constraints

- Admin effort.
- Capacity and licensing to verify.
- Compliance rules.
- Release independence.

## Options

| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Single shared environment | Simple, cheap | Blast radius, permission sprawl, coupled releases |
| Environment per application or team | Isolation, independent lifecycle | More admin, capacity and pipeline cost |
| Tiered: shared for low risk, isolated for sensitive or critical | Balanced | Needs clear tiering rules |

## Operational and organisational trade-offs

- Operations: more environments mean more pipelines and monitoring.
- Organisation: autonomy rises with isolation but consistency drops.
- Cost: capacity and licensing may rise.
- Security: isolation limits accidental exposure.

## Recommendation under stated assumptions

**Assumptions:** Mixed sensitivity, several teams and a small platform team.

**Recommendation:** Use the tiered model with explicit criteria, automation for creating isolated environments and standard policies applied to all.

## Evidence that would change the recommendation

- Incidents caused by shared permissions.
- Admin cost exceeding value.
- Compliance findings.
- Release conflicts between teams.

## ADR

```markdown
# ADR: Environment strategy
Status: Proposed
Context: Mixed sensitivity, several teams.
Decision: Tiered environments with documented criteria.
Consequences: Platform team automates provisioning.
Revisit when: Number of environments strains administration.
```

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- One environment per person.
- No clean-up of abandoned environments.
- Inconsistent policies between tiers.
followUps: How do you decide which tier an app belongs to?
How do you automate provisioning?
How do you clean up unused environments?

questions.title: Trade-off: native Power Platform ALM or external CI/CD orchestration?
questions.quick: I ask who releases, what testing and approval evidence is required, how many systems release together, and what skills the team has. Native tooling is quicker to set up and friendlier to makers; external CI/CD offers richer testing, branching, cross-system release and consistent policy but needs engineering effort. I would start native for simple solutions, use external orchestration where release complexity or audit demands justify it, and record an ADR.
questions.revision: Native ALM for simple, maker-led releases; external CI/CD for automated testing, branching and cross-system releases; choose by release complexity and audit needs.
questions.detailed:
A release-tooling decision that affects culture as much as technology.

## Business context

A platform with many solutions, some linked to external services that release in step.

## Clarifying questions

- How many solutions and teams?
- What testing gates are required?
- Do releases span systems?
- Who approves production?
- What skills exist?

## Constraints

- Current tooling investments.
- Audit evidence.
- Service principal management.
- Platform feature status to verify.

## Options

| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Native pipelines | Low setup, maker friendly | Limited custom gating, fewer cross-system steps |
| External CI/CD | Flexible, testable, uniform with other systems | Engineering effort, credentials management |
| Native for most, external for exceptions | Pragmatic | Two paths to support |

## Operational and organisational trade-offs

- Skills: external route needs pipeline engineers.
- Consistency with other engineering teams improves externally.
- Native is easier to hand over to makers.
- Both need solution layering and versioning discipline.

## Recommendation under stated assumptions

**Assumptions:** A mix of simple and cross-system solutions.

**Recommendation:** Native pipelines by default, external orchestration for solutions with automated test gates or cross-system releases, under one set of standards.

## Evidence that would change the recommendation

- Audit requirements native tooling cannot meet.
- Frequent cross-system release failures.
- Platform capability changes.

## ADR

```markdown
# ADR: Release approach for solutions
Status: Proposed
Context: Mixed complexity.
Decision: Native default; external for defined exceptions.
Consequences: Two documented paths.
Revisit when: Exceptions become the majority.
```

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Practical tip

Write the decision, the evidence behind it and the conditions for revisiting it in one short page, share it with the people affected before the meeting, and keep a dated log so the reasoning can be audited later.

## Common mistakes

- Building elaborate pipelines for simple apps.
- Hard-coded credentials in pipelines.
- No rollback plan.
followUps: How do you manage service principals safely?
How do you test a solution automatically?
What is your rollback story?

questions.title: Trade-off: one standard AI framework or several approved options?
questions.quick: I ask what problem standardisation solves: support cost, security review, skills transfer, or reuse, and what it would stop teams doing. One framework simplifies governance and training but can block valid needs; many options increase flexibility but fragment support. I would usually define one default, a short approved list with entry criteria, a common tool and observability layer, and an exception process, and record this in an ADR.
questions.revision: One default framework, a short approved list with entry criteria, shared tool and observability standards, and an exception process.
questions.detailed:
Platform teams constantly balance control against fit.

## Business context

Several teams are starting agent projects and each wants a different framework.

## Clarifying questions

- What support capacity do we have?
- What common needs exist, such as tracing and security review?
- Are use cases genuinely different?
- How quickly do frameworks change?
- What did past standardisation cost?

## Constraints

- Security review capacity.
- Training budget.
- Vendor roadmap uncertainty.
- Existing codebases.

## Options

| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Single mandated framework | Easy support and training | Misfit risk, vendor concentration |
| Free choice | Maximum team autonomy | Fragmentation, uneven security, duplicated effort |
| Default plus approved alternatives | Balance | Needs curation and criteria |

## Operational and organisational trade-offs

- Standardise the interfaces: tools, tracing, evaluation, secrets, rather than only the framework.
- Teams may resent mandates without a route to exceptions.
- Review capacity limits how many options can be supported.
- Frameworks change quickly so avoid deep lock-in.

## Recommendation under stated assumptions

**Assumptions:** Several teams, small COE, fast-moving ecosystem.

**Recommendation:** Choose a default, allow one or two alternatives that meet entry criteria, and standardise tool interfaces and observability so switching is cheap.

## Evidence that would change the recommendation

- Teams repeatedly needing the same exception.
- Support cost per framework.
- A framework losing vendor support.

## ADR

```markdown
# ADR: AI framework standardisation
Status: Proposed
Context: Multiple teams, small COE.
Decision: Default framework plus criteria-based alternatives.
Consequences: COE maintains templates and criteria.
Revisit when: Yearly or on major ecosystem change.
```

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Mandating without consultation.
- Standardising only the library, not the interfaces.
- No review date.
followUps: What are your entry criteria for an alternative?
How do you keep tool code portable?
How often would you review the standard?

questions.title: Trade-off: RAG over documents or structured API retrieval for an assistant?
questions.quick: I ask what the answers are made of: prose in documents, or facts in systems. RAG suits unstructured knowledge, policies and manuals; structured API or query retrieval suits live, exact, permissioned data such as balances or statuses where a wrong number is costly. Often both are needed, routed by question type. I would test on real questions, enforce permissions in either path, and record an ADR.
questions.revision: RAG for unstructured knowledge; structured API or query retrieval for exact, live, permissioned facts; route by question type and enforce permissions.
questions.detailed:
Retrieval method should follow the shape of the data, not fashion.

## Business context

An assistant must answer policy questions and also report account or order status.

## Clarifying questions

- What share of questions are about documents versus data?
- How fresh must answers be?
- What is the cost of a wrong answer?
- How are permissions enforced?
- Are citations required?

## Constraints

- Source system APIs.
- Index freshness.
- Permission model.
- Latency.

## Options

| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| RAG over indexed documents | Good for prose, citations | Stale index, weak for exact figures |
| Structured API or query tools | Exact, live, permissioned | Needs defined tools, limited to anticipated queries |
| Router using both | Covers both types | Routing errors, more to evaluate |

## Operational and organisational trade-offs

- Operations: indexes need refresh monitoring; APIs need rate limits.
- Organisation: content owners keep documents current.
- Security: filter by user permission at retrieval, not after.
- Evaluation sets should cover both paths.

## Recommendation under stated assumptions

**Assumptions:** Mixed questions, strict accuracy for figures, citation needed for policy.

**Recommendation:** Route policy questions to RAG with citations and factual questions to structured tools, with a safe fallback when routing is uncertain.

## Evidence that would change the recommendation

- Routing error rates in evaluation.
- Index staleness incidents.
- Share of questions in each class.

## ADR

```markdown
# ADR: Retrieval strategy for the assistant
Status: Proposed
Context: Mixed document and data questions.
Decision: Router with RAG and structured tools.
Consequences: Two evaluation sets; permissions in both.
Revisit when: Question mix shifts.
```

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Using RAG for numbers.
- Filtering permissions after retrieval.
- No evaluation for the router.
followUps: How do you evaluate routing?
How do you enforce permissions in RAG?
What if a question needs both?

questions.title: Trade-off: custom text-to-SQL or a managed analytics assistant such as Databricks Genie?
questions.quick: I ask how well modelled and documented the data is, how many users and questions there are, what governance applies, and how much control over behaviour is needed. A managed assistant gets value quickly on governed, well described data; a custom text-to-SQL service allows tailored prompts, semantic layers, validation and UX but needs ownership and evaluation. I would start managed, build custom only for a measured gap, and record an ADR. Verify current product capabilities.
questions.revision: Start managed on well-described governed data; build custom text-to-SQL only for a measured gap, always with permissions, validation and evaluation.
questions.detailed:
Natural-language analytics is both a product choice and a data-quality question.

## Business context

Business users want to ask questions of curated warehouse tables without waiting for analysts.

## Clarifying questions

- How well documented are tables and metrics?
- Who owns wrong answers?
- What permissions model exists?
- How varied are the questions?
- What is the budget?

## Constraints

- Governance and row-level security.
- Compute cost.
- Evaluation capacity.
- Vendor feature status.

## Options

| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Managed assistant | Fast, inherits platform permissions, less to run | Less control, feature limits |
| Custom text-to-SQL | Control of prompts, validation, UX | Build and evaluation effort, security responsibility |
| Managed assistant plus curated metrics layer | Better accuracy | Metric layer upkeep |

## Operational and organisational trade-offs

- Data teams must curate descriptions either way.
- Custom needs SQL validation, read-only roles and query limits.
- Wrong answers need a feedback and review loop.
- Users need to see the generated SQL or logic.

## Recommendation under stated assumptions

**Assumptions:** Reasonably modelled data, moderate users, strong governance needs.

**Recommendation:** Start with the managed assistant on curated tables; add a metrics layer; build custom only where evaluation shows a gap that matters.

## Evidence that would change the recommendation

- Accuracy below target on key questions.
- Need for UX or workflow the product cannot provide.
- Cost per query at scale.

## ADR

```markdown
# ADR: Natural-language analytics approach
Status: Proposed
Context: Curated tables, governed access.
Decision: Managed assistant first.
Consequences: Data team owns descriptions and review loop.
Revisit when: Evaluation gaps or cost.
```

Product capabilities, limits, licensing and preview status change often, so verify current vendor documentation before relying on any product claim here.

## Common mistakes

- Giving the model write access.
- No evaluation set.
- Skipping metric definitions.
followUps: How would you stop unsafe SQL?
How do you evaluate accuracy?
Who owns a wrong answer?

questions.title: Trade-off: build internally or adopt a managed service?
questions.quick: I ask whether the capability differentiates the business, how well a managed service fits, the run and exit costs, and what skills we have. Differentiating or highly specific capabilities may justify building; commodity capabilities usually favour adopting, since operations are the hidden cost. I compare total cost of ownership over a few years, check data and compliance fit, plan an exit route, and record an ADR with explicit review triggers.
questions.revision: Build what differentiates; adopt commodity capabilities, comparing multi-year total cost, compliance fit and exit options, with review triggers in the ADR.
questions.detailed:
The cost of building is visible; the cost of running is not.

## Business context

A team wants to build its own evaluation and monitoring tooling for AI applications.

## Clarifying questions

- Is this differentiating?
- What does the service not do?
- Data location and compliance?
- Run cost versus team cost?
- What is the exit path?

## Constraints

- Budget cycles.
- Procurement time.
- Skills and hiring.
- Security review.

## Options

| Option | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|

- Operations: building means on-call for it.
- Organisation: a built tool needs a long-lived owner.
- Lock-in is reduced by open formats and clean interfaces.
- Switching costs should be estimated up front.

## Recommendation under stated assumptions

**Assumptions:** Capability is commodity, team is small and compliance is satisfiable.

**Recommendation:** Adopt a managed service behind a thin internal interface, and build only the parts that encode our own policies.

- Compliance blockers.
- Costs growing faster than value.
- Vendor roadmap divergence.

## ADR

```markdown
# ADR: Evaluation tooling sourcing
Status: Proposed
Context: Commodity capability, small team.
Decision: Adopt managed service with thin wrapper.
Consequences: Vendor dependency, lower build effort.
Revisit when: Cost or compliance triggers.
```

Write the decision, the evidence behind it and the conditions for revisiting it in one short page, share it with the people affected before the meeting, and keep a dated log so the reasoning can be audited later.

- Ignoring exit cost.
- Underestimating integration work when adopting.

questions.title: An elegant solution exceeds the budget, and when is accepting technical debt right?
questions.quick: I separate what is essential from what is elegant. I ask which requirements must be met now, what the cost of the shortcut is later, and whether it is reversible. Accepting debt is right when it buys learning or time-to-market, is deliberate, small, owned, recorded with a repayment trigger, and does not touch security or data integrity. I propose a staged design: the minimal version now, with seams for the elegant one.

questions.title: How do you prove an architecture is production-ready? Give a readiness review checklist
questions.quick: I use an evidence-based readiness review, not opinion. For each area, the team shows proof: requirements and SLOs, security and data review, tested failure and recovery, load tests against targets, monitoring and alerting with runbooks, deployment and rollback, cost estimate, ownership and on-call, and for AI systems an evaluation set and guardrail tests. diagrams.title: Readiness review gates
diagrams.alt: The architecture passes through readiness gates covering requirements, security, resilience, performance, operations and cost. Each gate needs evidence. Critical gaps block launch, while accepted risks are recorded and owned.

questions.detailed:
Production readiness means evidence that the system meets its objectives and that people can run it, not that it works in a demo.

{{diagram:ready-gates}}

## Readiness checklist

| Area | Evidence expected |
|---|---|
| Requirements | Agreed SLOs, scale targets, data classification |
| Security | Threat model, identity and least privilege, secrets handling, penetration or review findings closed |
| Data | Backup, restore tested, retention, residency, privacy review |
| Resilience | Failure injection results, timeouts, retries, idempotency, dependency outage behaviour |
| Performance | Load test against target with <measured value> results and headroom |
| Observability | Metrics, logs, traces, dashboards, alerts tied to SLOs |
| Operations | Runbooks, on-call owner, incident process, escalation |
| Deployment | Automated pipeline, rollback tested, environment parity |
| Cost | Forecast and budget alerts |
| Compliance | Audit trail and approvals |
| AI components | Evaluation set results, guardrail and prompt-injection tests, human oversight, model change process |
| Support | Documentation, training, known limitations |

## Running the review

1. Agree the checklist early so teams build to it.
2. Hold the review with a mix of architects, security, operations and the product owner.
3. Classify gaps as blocker, must-fix-soon or accepted risk.
4. Record accepted risks with an owner and review date.
5. Re-run after significant change.

## Evidence over assertion

"We have monitoring" is not evidence; a dashboard plus an alert that fired in a test is. "We can restore" is not evidence; a timed restore drill is.

Write the decision, the evidence behind it and the conditions for revisiting it in one short page, share it with the people affected before the meeting, and keep a dated log so the reasoning can be audited later.

- Treating readiness as a document exercise.
- Skipping rollback and restore tests.
- Launching with no named on-call owner.
- Forgetting cost and capacity limits.
- Letting the review become a rubber stamp under deadline pressure.

questions.title: A security requirement conflicts with a delivery deadline. What do you do?
questions.quick: I clarify the requirement and the actual risk, then look for options that satisfy it faster: reduce scope, phase the release, use an approved pattern, or add compensating controls.
